reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because its main purpose is to demonstrate transferring cryptocurrency from Coinbase to Binance, including checking the address and confirming the transfer. The creator also promotes signup referral links and says both parties would receive $10 in Bitcoin, but the video does not tie that offer to a deceptive claim or request for a payment or sensitive data.

opening.argument: The video makes a concrete asset promise conditional on a viewer action: use the creator's Coinbase referral link and sign up. The speaker says the viewer will receive $10 and that both parties receive $10, while the description supplies the referral link alongside the offer of free Bitcoin. That is not merely discussion of cryptocurrency; it is a direct acquisition pitch connecting registration with an easy-to-obtain digital-asset reward. The promised value and the requested signup are explicitly joined, matching a low-barrier reward solicitation.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The demonstration framing does not answer the promotional issue. Showing how to move funds can make the referral pitch more credible, but it does not remove the explicit promise of $10 for signing up. The defense itself acknowledges the referral offer and therefore confirms that the video asks viewers to register in exchange for digital-asset value.

citations.quote: if you guys use my referral link to sign up for Coinbase, you'll get $10 just for signing up for coinbase
GET $10 of free bitcoin- https://www.coinbase.com/join/59ed436ca0a8980300c43911

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted reward is a disclosed referral incentive, not evidence that the video falsely promises value. The material does not establish that the $10 offer is unavailable, fabricated, or deceptive; it only states the condition and the mutual benefit. The transfer instructions remain the video's stated subject, and a referral link does not by itself convert an operational demonstration into a scam.

citations.quote: In this video I teach how to transfer Ethereum from coinbase to binance.
well we both will get ten dollars and you will get ten dollars for just for signing up

opening.argument: Several risk signals appear together: cryptocurrency transfers, external signup links, and an unusually easy $10 digital-asset reward. The description advertises free Bitcoin through a Coinbase link, while the speaker says signing up alone earns $10 and directs viewers to use the referral link. The speaker also describes entering a wallet address, paying a network fee, and completing two-step verification before sending funds. Even if the mechanics are real, this combination places a simple reward solicitation next to a financial workflow involving wallets, fees, and authentication, encouraging participation through an attractive return.

citations.quote: GET $10 of free bitcoin- https://www.coinbase.com/join/59ed436ca0a8980300c43911
you'll get $10 just for signing up for coinbase
they do charge a network fee
enter the two-step verification code provided by your authentication app

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the content educational does not make these signals disappear. The video still pairs cryptocurrency handling and authentication with a free-value signup pitch, and the description places several external links beside that pitch. A careful viewer should treat that combination as promotional solicitation rather than infer safety merely because transfer steps are shown.

citations.quote: GET $10 of free bitcoin- https://www.coinbase.com/join/59ed436ca0a8980300c43911
if you guys use my referral link to sign up for Coinbase

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These are ordinary features of the demonstrated process, not proof of deception. The video warns that a mistaken transfer cannot be recovered and says a network fee is charged; it does not promise profit from sending funds. The $10 statement is a disclosed referral reward, and the sources do not show that viewers are asked to surrender credentials or pay to claim it.

opening.argument: Although presented as a transfer lesson, the video functions as a gateway to participation in the creator's linked services. The description gives a Coinbase referral link promising free Bitcoin, plus Binance and other promotional links. During the demonstration, the speaker repeatedly walks viewers through signing in, obtaining a deposit address, sending funds, and waiting for the transaction, then returns to the referral appeal and says the reward can cover fees or be used to buy cryptocurrency. The instructional wrapper therefore actively steers viewers toward registration and crypto activity rather than neutrally explaining the technology.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The stated subject does not control the video's practical effect. The speaker begins with account access and ends by urging viewers to use the referral reward for fees or cryptocurrency, while the description supplies multiple service links. Those details support reading the lesson as promotional steering, not as a detached explanation whose commercial component is incidental.
